title: Scenario-focused presets and runbook (draft)
content:
Purpose:
This memo captures a set of scenario-focused inference presets and an operational runbook for applying them during experiments and gradual rollouts. The goal is to give engineers and product owners compact, reproducible starting points (batch/cache/quantize + rollout recipe) and the steps to validate cost/quality tradeoffs with the cost model spreadsheet.

Scope and constraints:
- Presets are intended for Redwood inference runtime v3.x and above.
- Targeted model families: Llama-2/Redwood-Open variants, and transformer decoders used for chat/completion and embeddings.
- Presets assume observed request distributions (payloads/tokens) are roughly stable for the scenario; for heavy tail or extreme variability use the profiling runbook before applying.
- All numeric suggestions are conservative; run local microbenchmarks and the cost spreadsheet before full rollout.

High-level summary (short):
- Interactive low-latency (chat): small max-batch (1-4), short batch window (2–6 ms), KV/prefix cache enabled, use 8-bit quantization only for models that pass RMSE/QA regression gate.
- High-throughput batch generation: large batch sizes (32–128) with flexible batching window (20–80 ms), disable request-level caching; enable token-prefix caching if repeated prefixes are common; prefer 4-bit quantization when quality delta within tolerance.
- Embeddings / vector indexing: shardable micro-batching (16–64), aggressive KV cache and LRU eviction tuned by embedding fingerprinting; prefer int8 quant for throughput-vs-quality sweet spot.
- Regulated/private deployments: conservative quantization (no lossy 4-bit unless validated), longer canary windows, per-route observability and audit logging enabled.

Preset details (scenario cards):
1) Interactive chat - low latency (web chat, < 150ms p95 target)
- batch_size: target 1–4 (max 8), prefer 2 for bursty traffic
- max_batch_latency_ms: 3–6 ms
- batching_mode: dynamic continuous batching with immediate flush on end-of-turn token
- cache_policy: prefix cache enabled for user system messages and common instructions; KV cache enabled across tokens for same conversation; cache_ttl: 5m for short-lived sessions, 24h for persistent bots with privacy ok
- quantization: q8hf or int8 as first pass; q4 variants only after quality gate
- fallback: route to a larger model variant if observed QPS saturates or latency SLO violated
- evaluation metrics to run: p50/p95 latency, generation perplexity drift vs baseline, user-facing correctness tests (10 small prompt set)

2) Bulk generation - high throughput (offline jobs, N requests batched)
- batch_size: 64–128 (configurable per GPU model)
- max_batch_latency_ms: 30–80 ms
- batching_mode: large-window batching with token-aware splitting for very long prompts
- cache_policy: enable prefix caching for repeated templates; disable per-request caches that block batching aggregation
- quantization: q4x-compatible quant (4-bit) with calibration on representative dataset; track BLEU/ROUGE shifts if applicable
- evaluation metrics: throughput (tokens/s), GPU utilization curve, cost per 1M tokens from spreadsheet, generation quality regression tests

3) Embeddings at scale (search/indexing pipelines)
- micro_batch_size: 16–64 per worker, accumulate gradients off
- cache_policy: content-hash keying, allow multi-hour TTL for hot vectors, shard cache by namespace to control eviction
- quantization: int8 for embedding projection layers; careful not to quantize normalization layers unless tested
- evaluation: cosine-sim stability, recall@k changes, index build time improvement, cost per 1M embeddings

4) On-prem / constrained-GPU (single A10 / H100 small pods)
- batch_size: tuned to device memory (empirically determined); start at 8 for A10, 16 for H100 with q8-int8
- cache_policy: local in-memory cache with optional shared redis for larger clusters; keep TTL conservative (1h) to avoid memory thrash
- quantization: favor q8/int8; enable mixed-precision kernels
- evaluation: memory footprint, OOM rate, tail-latency p99, and cost-model delta vs hosted baseline

Runbook: how to apply a preset safely
Step 0 - profile: run the sampling profiler for 30–60 minutes against real traffic sample and produce: token distribution histogram, sequence length percentiles, prefix repetition frequency, and request arrival distribution. Feed these into the cost spreadsheet.
Step 1 - pick preset and simulate: copy preset values to the cost-model spreadsheet scenario tab. Run the nominal and pessimistic columns (p50, p95).
Step 2 - microbenchmark: deploy to a single dedicated node (canary) with observability hooks: token-level cost logging, per-request lat/trace ids, and quality sampler (10–100 sampled prompts). Run for at least 1 hour of representative load.
Step 3 - compare quality and cost: compare baseline and candidate vs metrics: p50/p95 latency, throughput, cost per 1M tokens, and quality delta (perplexity or task-specific metric). If quality delta exceeds tolerances, iterate quantization or reduce batch size.
Step 4 - canary rollout: 5% traffic for 24 hours (longer for regulated flows). Monitor error rates, tail-latency, and key business metrics.
Step 5 - ramp schedule: 5 -> 20 -> 50 -> 100 over multiple windows (24–48h), unless automated rollback triggers fire.
Step 6 - postmortem and lesson capture: capture the run into a shared spreadsheet tab plus quick notes in the runbook and create a PR to codify the chosen preset into Redwood Optimize presets library.

Monitoring thresholds and automated rollback triggers (recommended defaults)
- latency p95 increase > 20% vs baseline -> pause rollout and revert to last good config
- error rate increase (5xx or model decode failures) > 0.5% absolute -> immediate rollback
- quality regression (task metric drop) > pre-agreed threshold (e.g., 3% task_accuracy) -> rollback and disable quantization automatically

Cost spreadsheet walkthrough (quick):
Essential columns to edit for each preset: model_name, qconfig (none/q8/q4), tokens_per_request_p50/p95, avg_response_tokens, batch_window_ms, empirical_throughput_tokens_per_gpu, gpu_cost_per_hour, cache_hit_rate, cache_effective_token_savings.
Derived outputs to inspect: effective_cost_per_1M_tokens, expected_inference_latency_p50/p95, GPU_utilization_margin, and break-even point vs hosted pricing.
Tips: run two columns for pessimistic and optimistic cache-hit assumptions (+/- 15%). For quantized runs, include an accuracy penalty fraction column to model potential re-run costs if responses degrade and require additional post-processing.

Quality gates and validation checklist:
- Run the small evaluation suite (50 labelled prompts) and ensure no >2% regression on key metrics before canary.
- Run subjective review (3 human raters) for any q4 deployment in production.
- Confirm reproducibility: same prompt batch re-run should produce stable latency and token-cost numbers within 5%.

Open questions and caveats:
- Long-context models with huge KV caches: how to account for cross-request reuse vs memory pressure in cluster sizing? (need a microexperiment for 1M-conversation KV footprint).
- Embedding quantization impact on semantic similarity in low-resource languages needs a focused eval.
- Some third-party models show unforeseen failure modes under q4; require model-onboarding checklist update.

Next steps (action items):
- Run profiling job for priority customer flows by 2025-02-14 (owner: Marcus Lee).
- Add two new columns to the cost spreadsheet for per-request cache_ttl and KV_shard_count (owner: Elena Martinez).
- Create a Redwood Optimize preset PR and link to this memo after successful canary (owner: Ravi Desai).

References and inspiration:
- internal spreadsheet: linked_artifacts above
- Related internal drafts: profiling-driven-inference-ladder-notes (see product/optimize), latency-aware batching presets doc: internal repo

Appendix: short example run (toy numbers)
Scenario: web chat 10k daily active users, avg 30 tokens per turn, 3 turns per session.
- baseline (no quant, no cache): cost_per_1M_tokens = $X (see sheet), p95 latency = 210ms
- candidate (int8 + prefix cache 30% hit + batch window 4ms): expected cost_per_1M_tokens = baseline * 0.62, p95 latency = 145ms.
Notes: this toy run assumes model q8 passes the quality gate. If q4 is required, add a quality penalty budget in the spreadsheet.
